text:
What do you do for your skin beyond cosmetics and skincare devices? [Routine Help]

I’m curious about habits and small changes people find helpful.

I am 45, rosacea, seb derm, actinic keratoses (sun sensitive). I live in Scandinavia, and I find winter most challenhing. Here are a few things I do:

- UV protection: UPF clothing, a hat and big sunglasses.

- a pillow that doesn’t squish my face: I sleep on a Sleep & Glow pillow to reduce how much my face gets pressed into the pillow overnight. A smooth cover (satin/silk) also helps keep my hair from getting tangled.

- pillow bra at night: I wear one with the aim of reducing creasing on my chest while I sleep

- humidifier in the bedroom during winter: To help with dry air overnight.

- Gauze for drying my face: I use gauze to pat dry instead of a towel.

- wearing a buff that covers my face when it’s freezing outside (my seb derm often flares with heavy moisturizers)

- wash my face after washing my hair to remove shampoo and conditioner residue

- starting wearing gloves when I wouldn’t need them for cold protection yet, to protect my hands

[Sun Care] Sunscreen Reviews from my Spring/Summer 2026

I’ve been traveling a lot in the past 8 months and wanted to find the perfect Asian sunscreen. I’m mixed race and tan super easily. My sink is also dry/combo. I found the Japanese ones work best for me. The ethanol seems to help it to stop pilling on me but it might irritate others, so YMMV. Hope this helps folks out there.

All reviews here:

Biore Uv Aqua Rich Watery Essence 🇯🇵 - 9/10
Absorbs well. Has a bit of a grainy quality but it’s extremely slight. Doesn’t really add moisture to the skin. Fine to reapply during the day and waterproof. Never used on face.

Biore Athlizm Spray 🇯🇵 - 6/10 It’s fine, it is just a bad value for the money. The spray evaporates really quickly so it’s hard to tell where you applied it. Must prefer the cream

Biore Athlizm Cream 🇯🇵 - 9/10 Really the GOAT for anything outdoor, sweaty or swimming. You feel like a duck with it on. It stuck all day when I was in Singapore or swimming in the hottest days in Seattle. Not an everyday sunscreen, but the best for what it does.

Haruharu wonder black rice airyfit 🇰🇷 - 3/10
It piles on the face and body for me. Not waterproof so maybe best in winter. It may have to do with me putting too much on, but despite all the hype around it, wouldn’t buy it again

Nivea UV super water gel 🇯🇵 - 8/10
goes on very easily and disappears into the skin. Like the pump that you can refill. Not waterproof so prob best for winter/cooler months.

Mediheal Madecassoside moisture sun serum 🇰🇷 - 7/10
Applies as a liquid but absorbs instantly. You don’t need to reapply during the day. Waterproof and pretty much invisible. It does pill like every other Korean sunscreen on me. Wish it didn’t.

Holika Holika aloe waterproof sunscreen 🇰🇷 - 9/10
Smells pleasant like aloe vera. Ok to reapply throughout the day without piling. Leaves a very slight white cast in the elbow but that’s about all I can say bad about it. Didn’t use it on my face.

House of Hur Weightless 🇰🇷 - 5/10
No smell. Goes on very liquid and disappears with no glow. It seems to pill on the face around the neck but not on the body.

Senka UV water Gel 🇯🇵 - 7/10
It goes on a bit sticky but does dry. Leaves a white cast as it has zinc oxide in it. Def feels waterproof. Would use this in hot weather or swimming for sure. No smell. Fine to reapply.

Beauty of Joseon Relief Sun Aqua Fresh 🇰🇷 - 5/10
It pills on the face, back of the neck and ears but it’s fine on the body. Feels like lotion on the body so I like that.

KISS ME MOMMY! UV Aqua Milk Sunscreen SPF50+ PA++++ 🇯🇵 - 8/10
It’s waterproof, it dissolves into the skin, it’s great for the face. It does pill a little bit on my neck when I reapplied. It has no scent and it’s mild enough to use on a 1 year old baby.

SCINIC Enjoy Super Mild Sun Essence 🇰🇷 - 8/10 Great on first application, but it does pile on second application after a while. No white cast. No smell. Very light. Not waterproof. Does pile less than some others, will try applying less. Really want to love this one!

Nivea UV Super Water Essence EX 🇯🇵 - 9/10 Wonderful smell. Goes on like a creamy gel then disappears. Fine to reapply. Love it! Fine on face, but it is pretty shiny.

Skin Aqua Super Moisture UV Gel 🇯🇵 - 10/10 Great on face or body. Fine to reapply without pilling as it is a fine gel-like cream. Not too shiny. Waterproof. Very moisturizing ingredient list so works as a lotion. Might be perfect.

Biore Aqua Rich Watery Gel 🇯🇵 1/10 - Has titanium dioxide which immediately made me look sickly white. It also pills up on the skin after first application with no other product underneath. I thought I couldn’t dislike any Japanese sunscreen but here I am.

Nivea Deep Protect & Care gel 🇯🇵 - 8/10 Feels very moisturizing on my skin. I like the scent but it does smell like mosquito repellent when you put it on. Don’t know if I’m going to try it on face for that reason. Feels like I have nothing on after applying. Really good body sunscreen.

Biore UV Aqua Rich Airy Hold Cream 🇯🇵 - 5/10 Goes on very thick, like soft serve ice cream or Greek yogurt. At first it leaves a white tint, but you can rub it in. It doesn’t feel moisturizing per se but def feels like it’s sticking to your skin. Has titanium dioxide so I don’t think I’d use it on my face. I’ll use it up on my body but wouldn’t buy again.

Nivea UV Super Water Gel Ex 🇯🇵 - 10/10 Big ass bottle at 270g. Good deals on Yami. Goes on matte. Fine to reapply. Need to try on face.

Tage Cica-Tree Water Jelly Sun Serum 🇰🇷 - 6/10 It’s ok. It does pill a little around the folds of my neck upon reapplication, but that’s it. It goes on a bit shiny. The consistency is a bit chunky so it doesn’t come out of the tube consistently. It can come out a lot at once and it’s impossible to avoid. Wouldn’t buy again.

Nivea Men Uv Protector 🇯🇵 - 4/10 Too small. Smells funny. Pills on me on first application.

Kose Suncut Uv Perfect Essence 🇯🇵 - 7/10 Great size. Really moisturizing. Goes into skin and beard well. It does pill a little around my neck after reapplication. Great ingredients like Squalane and other soothing extracts.

Hatomugi UV care and moisturizing spf 50+ 🇯🇵 - 9/10 Big bottle. Very pleasant feeling and smell on the skin. Seemed fine on face. Doesn’t seem to be waterproof but great for daily use.

Nivea UV Super Water Essence Ex 🇯🇵 - 10/10 Really just as good as the gel. Slightly more moisturizing and a little less product for the money. Regardless, you put it on and a second later you’d never know it was on your face. Can reapply all day without pilling

[Personal] I truly believe that for the vast majority of people, you can make a good routine with relatively affordable products.

(This is just my opinion and my opinion only! Do not be offended if this does not apply to you!)

I see so many influencers and people recommending luxury items that cost hundreds of dollars or close to a hundred dollars for a small jar of 50ml face cream. I truly believe that for the overwhelming majority of people, you can make a suitable, multi-step routine with relatively affordable products that are perfectly safe for your skin!!

When I was just starting to take care of my skin, I was extremely overwhelmed because the thought of shelling out a hundred dollars for a tiny jar of face moisturizer repeatedly did not make me happy, let alone the other products like toners and serums sunscreens.

These days, there's so many relatively affordable products (even though it is getting increasingly expensive), like Neutrogena face washes, a ton of stuff from Cerave, Cetapil, and even other drugstore brands like Garnier and e.l.f. are coming out with fragrance free, gentle options. The Ordinary is especially good too, because they have so many affordable options.

This is with the caveat that i say relatively affordable because I still think that 20 dollars for a sunscreen is kind of a lot, but it's not like luxury levels of prices where you need to sell a kidney or something.

Currently, I can use a multistep routine with a hydrating toner, serums for targeted skin concerns, moisturizers, and also cleansers like oils and micellar waters and foaming face washes. Nothing I use is particularly expensive and it comes in large sizes so it lasts quite a while too. Everything I use is from the drugstore.

All in all, I genuinely believe that expensive skincare is a huge marketing ploy, and you don't need to pay those prices if you don't want to! This next sentence is not meant to sound judgemental, but a lot of expensive things have got to be deinfluenced because those prices are ridiculous, IMO!!

Do you think that most people can make a perfectly good routine with relatively affordable stuff?

I also think the barrier serum category isn’t as developed compared to Western brands. ocokind barrier serum, byoma barrier serum, theramide ceramide treatment etc. Like korea has great hydration game just lacks at lipid replenishment currently. The facial oil market also feels less developed. K-beauty's got some nice hydrating serums like iunik beta glucan but I feel like there's some glycerin based serums like prequel multi-quench, transparent labs, regimen labs etc are far more effective options.

Same with sunscreens. Many K-beauty sunscreens prioritize that elegant lightweight, matte, invisible finish, which I understand is popular. Anyways in the end it's just my opinion inspired by personal experience and I mean no offense. Feel free to share yours.

[Routine Help] Simple *but effective* skin care routine

TL;DR: 25F with dry, acne-prone skin. Recently stripped my routine down to just hydration and soothing basics. Skin is calm but I want to target pore size, brightening/PIH, and anti-aging. Do I risk adding actives back in, or leave it alone?

My Skin Type & History

Type: Dry, sensitive, and acne-prone. My skin feels tight after almost every cleanser, and I get occasional flaky/gritty skin on my forehead, but no intense overall oiliness.

History: Struggled with acne since age 11. I used to do a complex, multi-step routine (heavily inspired by Ashley Mixon), my skin was glowy/shiny - like light reflective, but I still had redness/sensitivity, acne, PIH. i felt like I was using a ton of products and not seeing any crazy results.

Past Actives: Used a custom prescription (0.05% Tretinoin / 2% Niacinamide / 8% Azelaic Acid) a few years ago for about 6-9months, just didn’t see much if a difference so I stopped using.

Current Routine (K-Beauty Focus)
My skin has been much calmer since cutting back to these basics:

AM: SKIN1004 Centella Ampoule Foam → CosRX Snail Mucin Essence → SKIN1004 Centella Soothing Cream → Beauty of Joseon Sunscreen.

PM: Anua Heartleaf Cleansing Oil → SKIN1004 Foam → CosRX Snail Mucin → Dear, Klairs Midnight Blue Calming Cream.

I also just started using the thayers milky toner mist here and there for added moisture, I like it so far I think.

My Goals
I want to target brightening/PIH, pore-minimizing, gentle exfoliation, and anti-aging without triggering breakouts or ruining my skin barrier.

The Dilemma & Ingredients I'm Considering:
Ingredients I dislike: Vitamin C and Niacinamide generally don't work for me and cause breakouts - I’ve tried a few formulations (though I’m mildly curious about the Then I Met You Giving Essence despite it having niacinamide). I didn’t really like the anua azelaic acid and everyone raves about it. I’m wondering if azelaic acid is another problem ingredient for me?

What I'm eyeing: The Farmacy Brighten Up Toner (TXA/Azelaic acid blend) for gentle exfoliation and brightening.

The Tret Route: Considering going back to Tretinoin, potentially paired with Azelaic Acid.

My question for you all:
Since my skin is doing pretty well right now, should I risk incorporating new products to reach that next "glass skin" level, or should I just quit while I'm ahead? If I do add something, what would you suggest based on my sensitivities? I prefer K-beauty, but mainly I want clean, high quality, evidenced based ingredients. I don’t have the skin type where I can just play around and slap anything on and have it work for me so I am very careful trying products - hence why I went back to basics with my routine. I still want a mostly simple routine, I want core, holy grail, multi use products. I don’t want to have to get a million things in order to get all the ingredients I want. I have considered skin cycling again, I work night shift at the moment so skin cycling is hard/confusing with an ever changing schedule, but I am transitioning to dayshift so I night be able to try that again. I am happy to take advice, discuss products/give me recommendations, but if you do have suggestions, let me know how to best incorporate them. :)

[PSA] Stay away from SA (BHA) if you are allergic to aspirin!

Posting this because neither my doctor nor my dermatologist ever warned me, and I spent years needlessly wrecking my skin. Every time I used salicylic acid (BHA) for face or body acne, I’d break out in clusters of angry, red, inflamed bumps. Everyone in skincare spaces always says "it's just a purge, push through it!" so I did. Turns out: aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid. If you have an allergy or cross-sensitivity to aspirin and other NSAIDs like I do, you're likely sensitive to salicylates in general. I only connected the dots when I had stomach issues and randomly read the warning label on a bottle of Pepto-Bismol (bismuth subsalicylate), which explicitly says not to take it if you're allergic to aspirin. I looked at the BHA products on my shelf and felt like an idiot.
label: psa_warning

text:
[Acne] Stopping Azelaic Acid Was the Best Thing I Did For My Skin

Azeliac Acid saved my skin.

I had bad acne in my late teens to early twenties (19-21) and was prescribed tretinoin. After about 8 months of consistent use, my acne started to clear up to a few small breakouts a week. However, I was left with PIE all over my face and I constantly looked like I was blushing. My dermatologist then prescribed me 15% AzA in conjunction with the tret, and not only did the PIE start to fade, but it put me over the finish line in terms of my acne and I barely, if ever, broke out.

I also have very dry skin. Since starting the tret I have had to slug with vaseline every night. If I skipped, my skin as very dry and flakey the next day. I have been doing this for years. A few times I tried to stop as the tret flakiness is not supposed to last years, but when I ceased for consecutive nights, I would experience sunburn level peeling. It was embarrassing. Even with slugging, certain areas of my face were very prone to flakiness. I carried lotion on me all the time. At work or school, wherever I was, if I noticed an area was dry I reapplied.

I was so confused why my skin never fully acclimated to tret. It worked perfectly on stopping acne and it even gave me the tret glow, yet I was plagued by the dryness. The slugging has been burdensome over the years too. Impromptu sleepovers made me dry as a snake the next day. Sleeping over a SO house was also a no no for slugging... was trying to not weird them out instantly. Sometimes it also felt a overstimulating. If it was hot in the night I could feel myself sweat through it and it would keep me up. Pillowcases have also needed to be changed more frequently for the buildup of grease.

Now to today. My AzA prescription was out of stock when I tried to refill it around Sept 1. The drugstore told me it was backordered until about mid-October. I tried to transfer it to another pharmacy and had some trouble doing so. I also attempted this refill after I had already run out and had not been using it for a few days (procrastination).

Over a month has passed of me not using AzA anymore. And my skin? Zero flakes. I noticed after an unplanned sleepover that I was not dry the next day. Some laziness the following night lead to me not slugging and I noticed the next day--still no flakes. I have not slugged in a month. I have no flakiness during the day. I've had to apply mid day lotion maybe once or twice the entire month.

Im putting this out here to remind everyone that sometimes our skincare has exhausted its benefit. AzA saved my skin and cleared all my PIE. Years after starting, stopping was the best thing I've done in a while for my skin. And yes, no breakouts either since ending AzA (tret is doing its job!)

text:
[PSA] Climate matters more than you think.

Basically, want to mention my own experience with my climate and how it dictated how my skin reacted to products.

I previously lived in a super humid environment before moving to a very dry one. I've practically always had breakouts despite everything I did. Generally, I didn't know how to take care of my skin.

Because of this, when I moved to an area with a dryer climate, I still had the impression that my skin was acne-prone and oily. Well, it seemed so because at this point I used less moisturizer and used harsh cleansers. My skin got much, much worse and even more oily.

Only recently did I realize that my climate was very drying. On social media, western standards of beauty are very common. I may not phrase this effectively, but what I mean is: people who live in very humid areas promote skin products that work for them. However, the same products may not work on you: not only because of your skin type, but also due to your climate. So, I just wanted to say that you should first look at your surroundings before falling for and buying every single product online.

For example, I started using 2 toners with heavy moisturizer + vaseline (PM and AM), and my skin didn't break out at all. In fact, oil production was reduced whereas my breakouts appeared less frequently. For some, this routine may wreak havoc on their skin, but it worked for me and that's what matters.

In conclusion, don't follow trends blindly and be mindful of the factors that affect YOUR skin. Everyone's skin is different so some things may not work for you as they work for others. Sorry if this post was a bit too long, I just wanted to share my experience and give some advice to others suffering from the same problems.

text:
Dix Hectares - The "Grand Cru" Skincare Scam [PSA]

Hey everyone,

Before I go into this, I have a background in wine, and while I won't say I have a "passion" for skincare (that sounds a bit corny to me personally), I enjoy it and I understand why people buy what they buy.

I'll even indulge a good marketing campaign from time to time (cough La Mer cough Augustinus Bader), go in with a "hey, you never know" attitude, and try to have some fun with it.

That being said, I went on Niche Beauty today and saw a new product from a brand called Dix Hectares which translates into "ten hectares". A hectare is a term used when measuring the size of a vineyard and is equal to 10,000 square meters. Given its name, I was naturally interested in the brand overall.

When reading the product description for The Seasonal Cream Autumn-Winter, priced at $357, on Niche Beauty, I came across this sentence:

    "The GEO3Active™ matrix—Angelica osmolytes, aquaporin-inducing rye, and lupin peptides, with seasonal botanicals grown on the Grand Cru estate".

This is when I thought "wow, this doesn't make any sense whatsoever". Now, before you think I'm just a "hater", let me explain:
Who's behind Dix Hectares

Let's start with who founded Dix Hectares: Charlotte Bouygues. Charlotte Bouygues is the daughter of Martin Bouygues who, in 2006, acquired Château Montrose together with his brother Olivier. Montrose is located in the Saint-Estèphe subregion of Bordeaux.

Charlotte graduated from Babson College with a BA in Business Administration. She then spent roughly three years at a beauty company that isn't considered luxury, so the filters will remove this post if I name it. I'll give you a hint: it rhymes with f'Oréal.

There she worked as an intern and participated in the Management Development Program. After that she headed advertising sales at TF1 Publicité, moved to TF1's programming team, then ran e-commerce at Aufeminin (a TF1 subsidiary) from 2019 to 2021 before joining her family's holding company, SCDM. She is now president of Eutopia Estates, the Bouygues family's wine division (seven properties) of SCDM.

My point in saying this: her career has primarily focused on brand marketing, advertising, e-commerce, and commercial strategy rather than chemistry, cosmetic formulation, or technical R&D. Marketing appears to be her strong suit, which is a core component to understanding what's going on here. That being said, no complaints so far.
The state of the wine industry

Now that we have a bit of background on the founder of Dix Hectares, let me paint you a picture of the current global wine market:

In short, it's going down the tubes.

There is a severe under-consumption/over-supply issue that has some regions in a crisis to the point where producers are just ripping out vines entirely. One region where this practice is prevalent is Bordeaux, where Château Montrose is located.

This drastic shift in consumer demand has also meant that Bordeaux's En Primeur system (where buyers purchase wine that isn't bottled yet at discounted prices, which allows wineries to receive money in advance) is also not doing too hot. If you would like to read more about this, or think I'm making things up, click this.

This now means producers are having to find creative ways to generate income due to lack of demand for their products, most of which revolve around wine tourism.

To be fair, I can't prove Dix Hectares was born exactly for this reason. Charlotte started work on the brand in 2021, the parcel was prepared in summer 2022, and the vine pull-up scheme and the En Primeur flops came after, in 2023-24.

Though, a classified Bordeaux estate launching a non-wine luxury line in this climate should raise some questions in my opinion. I personally feel they predicted the post-covid nosedive of the overall wine market was coming and were trying to be proactive. Again, that's speculation, I do not have that confirmed.

And, quite frankly, I don't have a problem with it. That is, until we get to Dix Hectares' marketing strategy. This is where I find things manipulative and, quite frankly, deceptive.

Dix Hectares' "secret sauce", or competitive advantage for those of you who took a marketing course, appears to be the combined concepts of vertical integration and provenance. Provenance in the sense that all the botanicals used to make the plant extracts in Dix Hectares' products are grown on one specific 10 hectare parcel of Montrose's 125 hectare estate. Vertical integration in the sense that, along with growing their own plants, their R&D lab is also located near Château Montrose. Okay, so far I'm okay with what is going on here.
The "Second Grand Cru Classé"

Now, let's break down some of Dix Hectares' marketing copy. We'll start with their own website:

    "Forty years later, the estate was awarded the appellation of Second Grand Cru Classé, a distinction made all the more exceptional by the fact that it honored the youngest vineyard in the classification. This recognition reflects both the hard work of those who cultivate it and the unique qualities of this site."

→ True. Château Montrose was declared a second growth in the 1855 classification of Bordeaux.

Now, if you're asking "classified as a what? a growth? do I need to go to the doctor or something?" that's exactly where your mind should be at. And yes, please go for an annual physical at the very least.

Silliness aside, this is where things are going to get a little "wine geeky". Though, it is imperative to understand what this classification actually did, what it means in reality, and how it is being used to manipulate us.
What the 1855 classification actually is

The 1855 classification ranked producers in the order of "first growth" (Lafite, Latour, Haut-Brion, Margaux, with Mouton being added later in 1973) to "fifth growth". Think of how the Michelin Guide ranks restaurants, same concept at play here.

This classification was based solely on wine price at the time...

...not on a blind tasting to assess quality...

...not based on a soil composition analysis...

...only by the price per tonneau each château's wine had commanded at the time. Period. Full stop. End of sentence.

Fun fact: a tonneau is a term used in Bordeaux to measure the volume of wine. One tonneau is equivalent to 900 liters of wine (roughly 1,200 750ml bottles or four 225L barrels aka Bordeaux barrels... Burgundian barrels are 228L... okay being a nerd wasn't the point here, I digress).

All jokes aside, it is imperative to understand that the 1855 classification ranked châteaus specifically, not the land upon which the château sits.

I will say this one more time for the people in the back:

The 1855 classification ranked châteaus specifically, not the land upon which the château sits.

As Bordeaux is a blending culture, the region celebrates the winemaker's ability to blend different varieties versus the land the grapes were grown on. Burgundy, on the other hand, celebrates the land and the producer is secondary.

Why does this distinction matter? Why do I need to know all of this? I don't even drink wine, why should I care? Where's Old Man Jenkins?!

These are all great questions, let me explain:
Burgundy vs. Bordeaux: what "Grand Cru" means

In Burgundy, the term Grand Cru holds meaning in regards to land. It is a designation attached to a single plot of land that directly indicates quality. That is why vineyards such as Musigny, Chambertin and, of course, Romanée-Conti command such high prices, because the land itself dictates quality. The groundwork for the Burgundian classification system was laid by the monks who mapped and delineated the region's individual plots (climats) over centuries, codified by Dr. Jules Lavalle in 1855, and made official with the AOC system in 1936.

In Bordeaux, the term "Grand Cru" literally means nothing when it comes to land. There is no official document assessing whether the soil under Château Montrose is better or worse than the soil under Château Lafite, because that question was never asked.

The 1855 classification ranking belongs to the estate, not the ground. For example, Château Latour can buy a new vineyard and the parcel would be classified with the same designation as Château Latour, which in this case is as a first growth.

The 1855 Classification does not, on its own, support the ideology that a parcel owned by a classified château is somehow inherently superior to another's. That's not what they did here, nor does the region claim to have done this.
"Cultivated on a Grand Cru terroir"

Okay, now that we got the geekiness out of the way, let's move on to, you guessed it, more marketing copy! Let's go to a tagline on Dix Hectares' official website:

    "French skincare, cultivated on a Grand Cru terroir
    Developed in harmony with the seasons
    Designed for your skin longevity"

→ Manipulative to the point where it becomes a flat out lie.

First, terroir is the combination of a vineyard's soil, climate, topography, and other natural conditions that influence a wine's flavor profile and overall development. How we use the phrase "it's everything" is essentially how winemakers use the word terroir.

From what we learned about the 1855 Classification, we can conclude that the "terroir" is not Grand Cru, the château is Grand Cru. Calling this a "Grand Cru terroir" takes the prestige of Château Montrose's classification and transfers it to the physical land on which Montrose is founded on and Dix Hectares grows its skincare ingredients. That is not how this works, even in the slightest.

Nothing about the 1855 Classification states that plants grown on this land are inherently superior to plants grown somewhere else, much less that they make better skincare ingredients.

What makes my head spin is the fact that Dix Hectares is basically taking the Burgundian classification system, copy and pasting Bordeaux into it, and hoping nobody bothers to fact check it along the way. And she can't say it's due to ignorance or "I didn't know", Charlotte Bouygues sits on the board of the Conseil des Grands Crus Classés du Médoc, the official trade organization representing the producers in the 1855 Classification.

So to me, it comes across either as arrogance or as thinking we're too stupid to make this connection. Any way you put it, I don't like it.
The "open-air laboratory"

Okay, one last claim and then I'll stop. This last bit did make me giggle, and I do like giggling:

    "Too fertile for vines, which prefer more hostile soils, one of the estate's plots had been untouched. It was then that the idea was born to exploit its potential and use it as an open-air laboratory, where the botanical essences essential to the development of the Dix Hectares formulas now flourish."

→ The level of tomfoolery here has reached an all time high.

Let me translate this for you: "We have a plot of land we don't know what to do with." Nothing inherently false here, I just feel it's one of the best examples of massaging the truth via marketing I have seen to date.

But let's read it again, because it does more damage than Dix Hectares realizes. By their own admission, this parcel is the one piece of Montrose that has nothing to do with the classified wine, it's the land Montrose won't put vines on. The same page even says the plot sat unplanted for many years, So even if, by some stretch of the imagination, you gave them "Grand Cru terroir", the skincare plot is exactly the vineyard that has never produced a drop of "Grand Cru" wine. It has nothing to do with the classification system and I don't think Dix Hectares even realizes what they did here.

The website even has a section that says "Is It Possible To Visit The Parcel?" to which the answer is "Our farm is not currently open to the public. However, please feel free to send us a request. We would be happy to explore the possibility of welcoming you under the best possible conditions."

"Our farm is not currently open to the public..." is Dix Hectares trying to create an aura of exclusivity. By all means, go visit Château Montrose for its winemaking, it's truly some of the best in the region, and to explore Bordeaux along with its other producers. It's a magical place and winemakers need our support now more than ever.

For me, it's about exploring and preserving a culture. While we may not share the same values in the US, wine plays a big part of everyday life in Europe, and to see it vanish would be a shame considering all the hard work producers put into their land over hundreds of years and into making wine itself.

That being said, flying over 4,000 miles in a metal tube to go see some random plot of land that you somehow think is the pinnacle of farming because you fell for Dix Hectares' marketing scheme is insane.
What I'm trying to get at is...

I feel the skincare industry as a whole needs to focus less on storytelling and more on creating formulas that are effective, cosmetically elegant, and formulated well. I understand there's an emotional component to this, it's how a brand like La Prairie has become so popular and is still around today. But when the story doesn't make sense is when we start to see the cracks, and that just takes the fun out of skincare for me personally.

Personally, I would have loved to see Dix Hectares as a potential rival to Caudalie. There, and around that price point, Dix Hectares' competitive advantages actually make sense. Over time, I could potentially see them overtaking Caudalie if they capture a niche target audience initially and build it over time.

But going for the high-margin money grab from the start with a messy, illogical marketing campaign is what I hate to see, it's like brands like this think we're stupid and that we'll just throw money at anything. This is not the case, at least for me.

Some may argue, "well why not email them directly, why do this so publicly?" I chose this route because all brands need to see this, not just Dix Hectares. Brand building isn't about deception, it's about making a product or service that a target audience actually finds valuable. The consumer decides whether there is value in your product, not the brand.

In closing, thank you for coming to my TED Talk and, guess what, we found Old Man Jenkins 😊!

text:
[PSA] Some thoughts on Laneige's cruelty-free status in 2026.

The Laneige website currently says this in their FAQs:

"Amorepacific Corporation, the parent company of the Laneige brand, strictly prohibits animal testing having begun its commitment to alternative testing methods over 30 years ago.

We ourselves do not test on animals nor do we ask others to conduct animal testing for us. If obligated by law or regulatory bodies for reasons of safety, however, limited exceptions may apply."

Cruelty-Free Kitty confirms the last sentence by saying of Laneige as of 2026 "Brands who fall under this category could also be selling products where animal testing is required by law."

Historically, China is known for mandatory animal testing requirements. In 2021, imported cosmetics (general skincare and haircare only though) could be free of animal testing.

The US meanwhile has inconsistent laws on this subject across the country. But here like in Canada, customer awareness and pressure seems a huge factor to whether skincare brands become cruelty-free on their own.

In the EU too, there are recent regulations that ban sale of cosmetic products "where either the final formulation, ingredients or raw materials have been the subject of animal testing".

Also, 45 others countries have banned animal testing for cosmetics. Animal testing is NOT mandatory not fully banned in the ASEAN countries.

At the moment, Laneige doesn't have any certifications, whether only in some countries or globally, related to being cruelty-free and is definitely not vegan.

Laneige ingredients also include those that apparently can be considered questionable, according to ireadlabelsforyou.com. This means that Laneige cannot claim to be "clean" skincare either.

In short, Laneige is NOT a cruelty-free brand, imo.

[Review] I received some products to review from VT cosmetics a few months ago and this is my review

1. Garlic AC Reedle shot Spot Patch- (2/10)

The simplest of the products! I was pretty excited to try these because they were my first experience with anything containing spicules. They didn’t break me out, which is a big deal for me because I have dry, redness-prone skin and am prone to some hormonal acne around my chin. The spicules did cause a little stinging for a few seconds when I first applied them, but it was very mild and nothing uncomfortable.

Unfortunately, they didn’t really do anything for me.

I tried them on everything, deep seated zits, whiteheads, blackheads, different kinds of active spots, etc., but I couldn’t see any noticeable improvement.

I also gave the second strip of patches to my friend, who has very oily, acne-prone skin and a deeper/tanned skin tone. She also didn’t notice any effect and said they didn’t seem to make a difference to any of her active breakouts either. So unfortunately, this one was a miss for both of us.

2. Cica-exosome sheet mask box- (6/10)

It was also my first time trying an exosome product, and I really wanted to love it because I generally love cica-based products.

The essence itself is quite nice, a little richer than what works best for me, though. If I used it several days in a row, I would start feeling a little clogged, so I could only comfortably use it once or twice a week.

My bigger issue was actually the sheet mask material.The mask is noticeably thicker than most sheet masks. It feels completely fine when you first put it on, but within a few minutes, especially as it starts drying, the material begins to feel quite harsh against my skin. I usually only leave sheet masks on for under 10 minutes, but even within that time, it could become dry enough that the texture started irritating my skin.

Because I liked the idea of the sheet-mask boxes so much, I ended up buying the Cica PDRN daily sheet mask box last month, and I can review that one too since I’m currently about halfway through the box.

This one completely solves the issue I had with the sheet material. The sheets are much thinner, softer and more comfortable, and they don’t irritate my skin at all.

However, I have the opposite problem with the essence.

The essence is very lightweight, but too light. It doesn’t feel hydrating enough. My skin basically feels like I’ve put water on it and nothing else. I was actually hoping this would be the perfect middle ground because the Cica Exosome mask was slightly too emollient for me. Unfortunately, this one went too far in the other direction. For comparison, I think Torriden dive-in sheet masks really nail what I’m looking for in this category, lightweight but genuinely hydrating, without feeling heavy or cloggig.

3. VT comsetics azelaic acid serum- (4/10)

This was actually my first Azelaic Acid product! I wouldn’t normally describe my skin as extremely sensitive. I can use glycolic acid pretty frequently, including almost daily during summer and every other day during winter, without much trouble. However, I found this particular Azelaic Acid formula a little too strong for me over the long term. I was completely fine with it initially, but with continued use, I noticed that it started drying my skin out. I suspect this may have something to do with the overall formula because it contains several other active ingredients, including tea tree extract and spicules. For my skin, that combination ended up feeling like a little too much.

Another thing I found confusing is that the exact percentage of Azelaic Acid isn’t clearly stated. The packaging says “20” so I assume it’s intended to indicate 20%, but I’m not completely sure. If it is 20%, that may simply be more than my skin needs, especially alongside the other actives in the formula.

I eventually passed this one on to my oily-skinned friend again, and she’s actually enjoying it much more than I did!

4. PDRN Stick Balm- 10/10. No notes.

You absolutely nailed this one. It’s very occlusive, but somehow it still doesn’t clog my skin. I recently started using retinal, and this has become one of my favourite products to use as the final step in my routine or before bed. I wake up with genuinely glowy, comfortable skin. It’s also fantastic for touch-ups. I can apply it over sunscreen, makeup, basically whatever I already have on my face, and it doesn’t completely destroy everything underneath.

I’ve tried a few other balms in this category, including the Tatcha one. I think the Tatcha balm is more nourishing and I believe it contains around 20% squalane, but it’s also considerably more expensive. For the price point, I think the VT balm is fantastic. I actually ran out of my first one last month and I’m already on my second stick. That probably says everything.

And one extra thing for the VT cosmetics team if they're reading this rn- PLEASE stop putting niacinamide in everything

This is a request from me personally, but also something I know a lot of other people would appreciate. Please, please consider making more products without niacinamide.It was genuinely so difficult for me to choose four products from the range because it feels like more than 90% of VT Cosmetics products contain niacinamide. I completely understand having some products formulated with it because it’s a very popular ingredient, but it doesn’t need to be in everything. This is especially frustrating for people who are specifically looking for products marketed toward sensitive skin.

I actually made a post about this once and it received thousands of upvotes, with many people agreeing that they were frustrated by the lack of niacinamide-free options.And the Reedle Shot is probably the biggest example. There are so many different Reedle Shot variants, yet there doesn’t seem to a single one without niacinamide.  It would be amazing to have more options for people who either don’t tolerate niacinamide or simply prefer not to use it

text:
[Review] Torriden Dive-In Serum — not dramatic, but my skin seems much more consistent with it

I’ve been using the Torriden Dive-In Serum for a while now, and at first I honestly didn’t think it was doing that much. It’s lightweight, absorbs quickly, and feels hydrating, but there was never a dramatic “wow, my skin looks different” moment.

I have oily skin, and this is actually where I started noticing a difference. When I use it at night, I tend to wake up less oily than I do when I skip it.

My skin obviously still produces oil, but it doesn’t have that overly greasy, almost dehydrated feeling I sometimes get in the morning. It just feels more balanced — hydrated, but not heavy or greasy. I notice the difference the most on the mornings after I don’t use it.

Texture-wise, it’s very lightweight and sinks in quickly without leaving a sticky layer behind. I really like that because I’m not a fan of heavy or greasy serums, especially in warmer or more humid weather. It also layers really easily with the rest of my skincare.

Another thing I like is how gentle it feels on my skin. I haven’t experienced any stinging or irritation from it, and it’s fragrance-free. Obviously everyone’s skin reacts differently, but for me it’s been a very easy serum to use consistently without having to think much about it.

The downside is that it might be too lightweight for very dry skin. Even though it feels hydrating, I wouldn’t expect it to replace a richer moisturizer, especially in cold or dry weather.

Overall, this isn’t a serum that transformed my skin overnight. The difference is much more subtle than that. But my skin seems more balanced when I use it consistently, and I can actually tell when I’ve skipped it. That’s probably why I keep reaching for it.

I’d recommend it if you:
• have oily or combination skin but still want hydration
• hate heavy, greasy or sticky serums
• want something lightweight for everyday use
• prefer fragrance-free, gentle-feeling skincare
• like layering multiple skincare products

I’d probably skip it if you:
• have very dry skin and want something rich
• expect intense hydration from one product alone
• prefer thick, nourishing serums
• are looking for a treatment serum that targets a specific concern beyond hydration

text:
[PSA] What actually happens to your skin in the months after finishing Accutane

Finishing Accutane doesn't mean the skin changes stop. People often aren't prepared for what comes next because almost everything written about the drug covers being on it, not the months after.

The barrier is still in recovery well after the last dose. Accutane significantly reduces sebum and affects how the skin functions at a basic level, and that doesn't reverse overnight. For the first few months the skin is more reactive and sensitized than it'll eventually be. Things that were completely fine before treatment can be more irritating in this window, which catches people off guard when they try to pick their old routine back up.

The oil coming back is part of this too. Sebum production dials back up gradually after stopping. Oil returning isn't a sign that acne is building, its the glands waking up, which is expected. The two feel linked but aren't the same thing.

Marks take longer to shift than most people anticipate. The pink and red ones especially need consistent SPF for months before they start to visibly move, and the nothing is working feeling in that period is almost always about the timeline rather than the approach. One person described not noticing a meaningful difference until month eight, then looking back at early photos and being genuinely shocked by how much had changed. Progress in this window is real but mostly invisible day to day.

The routine itself is worth stripping back for a few months. AHAs, BHAs, vitamin C, and retinoids are generally recommended to wait on, retinoids specifically at three to six months minimum after the last dose. A barrier thats still rebuilding reacts more than one thats had time to recover, and rushing the reintroduction is where most post-treatment irritation comes from. Someone who'd been managing a complex active routine for years described it as 'really hard at first to do nothing but moisturize', but said stripping back was the right call. That instinct to actively fix things is real but the skin in this window mostly needs time, not more intervention.

SPF is the one thing thats genuinely useful throughout this whole period. For the marks, for photosensitivity that can persist for months after stopping, and for a barrier that benefits from not being repeatedly stressed by UV.

See your derm before reintroducing prescription actives or professional treatments. The right timeline depends on how your skin actually recovered, not a general estimate.

[PSA] If no acne products are helping, you may have a compromised skin barrier

I'm just speaking from my experience, and certainly there are a lot of factors that contribute to persistent acne, but there's no harm in testing this out:

For about two years, I had really persistent acne especially on my forehead. I tried everything from using spot treatments, benzoyl peroxide, niacinamide, using AHAs, BHAs, tea tree oil, more potent cleansers, even changing my hair products... nothing worked. My acne was persistent, painful and left scars everywhere, which I then had to fade with retinol (whose overuse, surprise, surprise, was the major driving force behind my acne).

Here are a few mistakes I did throughout the years as someone with very oily skin and an OCD against oiliness (Feel free to make fun of me for my mistakes, but let this be a cautionary tale for those doing similar things):

    Cleansing my face three times a day (I have very oily skin, and I hated going to bed with any oiliness on my face, so I'd cleanse in the morning, in the shower, and right before bed)

    Using overly potent cleansers and then not moisturizing properly (I loathed how moisturizers made my skin oily, so sometimes I'd straight up skip the moisturizing stage)

    Using too much retinol (by that I mean using anything more than a pea-sized dot in each application)

    Scrubbing too hard / too long with physical exfoliants

To identify whether you have a damaged skin barrier is simple: go cold turkey on all actives for two weeks. Wash your face twice a day with a mild cleanser and use your moisturizer twice a day. Make sure they contain no acne-treating ingredients - because that's how you determine whether it's a damaged skin barrier or something else. If your acne stops being inflamed or stops popping up, congratulations: that means you have a damaged skin barrier.

I've swapped over to La Roche Posay's cleanser and moisturizer for damaged skin, and for the first time in two years, my acne is healing and so is my skin. I can finally fade acne scars without producing more acnes.

For skin barrier revitalization, I cannot recommend enough the Cicaplast B5 series (balm if you have dry skin, gel if you have oily/combo skin). It is godsend for damaged skin barrier. I've also switched over to the Toleriane Purifying Foaming Cream, but I suppose any mild cleanser you used during the cold turkey period that did work would work.

[Personal] Three Accutane courses, every treatment going, and it was the treatments that broke my barrier, not the acne

Disclosure first: I'm working on a skincare brand. Nothing to sell, no link. But this started fifteen years before any of that.

Eczema, then acne, then everything anyone offered me. One cream after another, rounds of antibiotics, every laser going including CO2, and eventually three full courses of isotretinoin. Each time I believed this would be the one. Each time I was left with a little less of myself.

By the end the acne wasn't doing the damage anymore. Everything I'd used against it was. Moisturisers stung. My own tap water stung. And every product marketed at exactly that did nothing, which is its own particular kind of lonely — you've run out of things to try and the failure starts to feel like it's you.

Somewhere in there I stopped reading reviews and started reading papers. What I found was almost annoyingly simple: your barrier isn't made of ceramides. It's made of three lipids — ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids — and there's research suggesting an incomplete mixture can leave skin worse off than applying nothing at all. Then I looked at my own bathroom shelf. Ceramides on everything. Cholesterol on nothing.

I'm not saying those products don't work. Plenty of people get real relief from them and I'd never argue with someone's own skin.

I'm mostly here because I know this sub is full of people who have been through some version of the same thing, and honestly your experience is worth more to me than anything I've read. What broke your skin, what quietly fixed it, what you gave up on — any of it. If you've got a product that finally settled things and you're curious, I'd love to know what's on it, but no homework, I'm just glad to hear the story.

Happy to share the papers if anyone wants them.

[PSA] Always spot test new products. ALWAYS.

This is a cautionary tale.

I have skin of steel. I never react to anything, ever. Salicylic acid, physical exfoliants, vitamin C, retinoids, going straight to bed with seven layers of sunscreen and bug spray on my face because I'm too lazy to wash my face: nothing.

Regular routine: salicylic cleanser rubbed into face with a washcloth followed with face lotion with added SPF in the morning. Salicylic cleanser alternating with vitamin c exfoliant followed by a hydrating gel in the evening, except one night a week where I do salicylic cleanser followed by retinol cream and hydrating gel.

I recently decided to simplify my routine and swap the salicylic and vitamin c cleansers with a single, all purpose gentle cleanser. I've also been trying to save money and wanted a product that I could pick up any any old drugstore so I wouldn't have to deal with shipping or stock-outs with buying specialty products online. Did some googling, found a gentle cleanser within the brand I've been using with reviews talking about how gentle it is and how it's perfect for people with sensitive skin and did I mention it is really gentle?

Enter Niacinamide.

According to Google and Tik Tok and seemingly every beauty article under the sun, this spiteful little devil of an ingredient is anti-inflammatory, strengthens your skin barrier, improves your skin's appearance, and all the while it is super gentle and perfect for people who have sensitive skin or skin conditions. I do not have sensitive skin, I have never spot tested new products, and I definitely wasn't going to do so for a product that was marketed for sensitive skin. That would be silly.

I used the new cleanser four times. First skin was itchy, then itchier, then hot, then feeling and looking like an angry sunburn by the fourth time. Did a quick comparison of the ingredients with every other product I've ever used in my life (many) and lo and behold this is the first time niacinamide has ever touched my face. An itchy arm after a belated spot test confirmed my suspicions. It's been five days, my face is still painfully burnt and in a cruel twist is now reacting to everything, including plain water.

Current routine: morning and night, splash cool water on face, slather on the Vaseline until I shine like a diamond and feel like a greased pig, wallow in self-pity.

Moral of the story: ALWAYS SPOT TEST NEW PRODUCTS, no matter how impervious your skin might appear to be. And listen to your skin when it's telling you it's upset.

Small edit: the cleanser was Marcelle's Foaming Gel Cleanser.

    3. Coat your face in a few drops of a light oil. I use plain unscented mineral oil (baby oil) but you could also use a biological oil.

- Not water resistant (Although a partner with the brand has claimed that it’s 80-minutes water resistant, but the packaging hasn’t been updated)
- Filters: 3% Avobenzone, 6% Bemotrizinol, 15% Homosalate, 5% Octisalate. (This does also contain butyloctyl salicylate pretty high up on the ingredients.)
- Finish: Natural/somewhat glowy. Definitely not matte, but I’d say it’s still an improvement over the greasy, plastic-y shine that most American chemical sunscreens leave.
- Eye sting after upper and lower eyelid application: Felt fine for most of the day, but makes my eyes water a bit after about six hours.
- Rating: 8/10 (deducted one point for modest glow, plus another point for no official water resistance)

La Roche Posay UVDefense SPF 50
- 50ml/1.7fl oz
- Purchased at launch for $39.99 or $23.52/oz
- Not water resistant
- Filters: 3% Avobenzone, 2% Bemotrizinol, 11% Homosalate, 5% Octisalate, 6% Octocrylene. Hard to tell from the label alone, but I suspect that they’re using their proprietary Netlock technology, so this could be the Tinosorb S Lite Aqua “version” of Bemotrizinol, but I defer to chemists to determine if that’s true.
- Finish: Almost identical to the Neutrogena. Genuinely not sure I could tell them apart. The Neutrogena “feels” a bit creamier as it’s rubbing in, but they feel and look similar once they’ve dried down. I’m happy to report that this does not leave a white cast on me. Not sure why, but some of LRP’s chemical sunscreens (Melt in Milk and their newish Sport sunscreens) leave tiny white flecks on my skin. This one fortunately does not do that.
- Eye sting after upper and lower eyelid application: Bear in mind that I’ve used this only once, but it made my eyes water pretty soon after application (within an hour). My eyes are extremely sensitive, though. Even mineral sunscreens bother them. The only “safe” options for me are the European UVmune formulas.
- Rating: 7/10 (same shine and water resistance deductions as neutrogena, plus an additional point for cost)

Another huge similarity is that they’re being marketed almost identically: both brands are making UVA protection and antioxidant claims. Neutrogena claims (with in-vitro testing) 5x the UVA protection of EltaMD UV Clear SPF 46 and 1.5x the UVA protection of the Korean Beauty of Joseon Relief Sun SPF 50+ PA++++. La Roche Posay is claiming 1.5x the UVA protection of “Amazon’s #1 Sunscreen,” (which I think is EltaMD UV Clear) using in-vivo testing. Absolutely brutal that they’re both dunking on EltaMD lmao.

Overall, these are good sunscreens and significant improvements for the American market, but they’re not quite holy grails. Still, it’s a major win to get more robust and reliable UVA protection from the drugstore.
